title: Melting permafrost has birthed a new type of large landslide

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: A graduate student and her supervisor discuss a field study on thawing permafrost and landslide risks.

script.en: Professor, I’ve been reading about those massive landslides in the Northwest Territories. The ground there had been frozen for ages, yet it suddenly collapsed. I’m thinking of focusing my thesis on similar risks in our local alpine regions.

That’s a timely topic. But remember, permafrost isn’t just frozen dirt; it’s a complex system. Before you design your field study, you need to consider what triggers such sudden failures. Are you thinking about temperature monitoring or something else?

I was planning to install temperature sensors at different depths, and also map cracks on the surface. But I’m not sure how to link those observations to actual landslide events. The literature seems to suggest that wildfires decades ago might have started the process.

Exactly. The wildfire removes the insulating vegetation, allowing deeper warming. Then water seeps through cracks and thaws the frozen layer from below. That’s the mechanism those researchers proposed. But your local area hasn’t had recent wildfires, so you’d need to look at long-term climate trends instead.

So you mean I should compare sites with different histories of disturbance? That could be complicated, but I see the point. Maybe I can use satellite data to identify slow ground movement before a collapse.

That’s a smart approach. Satellite interferometry can detect subtle creeping. But don’t underestimate the difficulty of interpreting the data. You’ll need to combine it with ground truth. Also, make sure your project timeline is realistic; two years of monitoring might not capture a catastrophic event.
I understand. I’ll narrow the scope to one valley and focus on the relationship between thaw depth and surface cracks. I’ll draft a revised proposal by next week.
Good. And keep in mind that this isn’t just an academic exercise. These slides can dam rivers and threaten communities. Your work could inform early warning systems.

script.en: Across the Arctic, a silent transformation is underway. Ground that has remained frozen for thousands of years is beginning to thaw, and the consequences are not merely local. When permafrost degrades, it can release carbon dioxide and methane, gases that further warm the atmosphere. But the effects extend beyond greenhouse gas emissions, and thawing ground also loses its mechanical strength, turning solid foundations into unstable slurry. This threatens roads, pipelines, and buildings constructed on frozen soil, and scientists have recently identified a particularly dramatic hazard: permafrost detachment slides. Unlike gradual subsidence, these events mobilize enormous blocks of still-frozen earth, sometimes moving them hundreds of meters in minutes. The trigger often lies in processes set in motion decades earlier. Wildfires, for instance, can burn away the insulating vegetation, allowing summer heat to penetrate deeper. Cracks then form as the ground creeps, and water seeps down, thawing the base of the frozen layer from below. Eventually, the entire slab detaches and slides catastrophically, and such slides are not isolated curiosities. Satellite surveys in one Canadian region have revealed more than 150 similar scars, suggesting the phenomenon may be widespread wherever permafrost is thin and warm. The implications for northern communities are serious, and A single slide can dam a river, causing floods upstream and disrupting fish migration. It can also sever transportation links, leaving villages isolated for weeks, and yet predicting these events remains difficult. The slow creeping that precedes a slide may last for years, offering a window for monitoring. Researchers are now testing ground-based sensors and satellite radar to detect subtle movements. But early warning systems need reliable data and local cooperation. As one geologist put it, we are only beginning to understand what happens beneath the surface. The challenge is urgent, because the frozen ground that once seemed permanent is now changing faster than our models predicted.

sections.title: A New Class of Catastrophic Landslides
sections.passage:
In 2018, a colossal landslide in Canada’s Northwest Territories moved a volume of earth comparable to seven Great Pyramids of Giza, leaving a barren scar in the forest. What baffled scientists was that the slide had begun in ground that had been frozen solid for years. An analysis published in Geophysical Research Letters now identifies the event as a new class of catastrophic landslides, termed permafrost detachment slides.

The mechanism appears to be set in motion decades before the actual collapse. Wildfires can burn away the insulating vegetation, allowing summer heat to penetrate deeper. As the frozen ground warms, it begins to creep, forming tension cracks. Water then seeps through these cracks and reaches beneath the permafrost layer, thawing it from below. Over time, the entire frozen slab loses its grip and detaches catastrophically. This sequence challenges the traditional view that permafrost thaws only from the top down.

Field observations revealed that both the 2018 slide and a similar event in 2017 had initiated along flat sliding surfaces roughly 20 meters underground, at the base of the permafrost layer. Satellite data showed that the ground at both sites had been gradually moving meters each year for decades. To test their hypothesis, researchers installed instruments that tracked ground temperature from 2020 to 2022, focusing on spots with undisturbed forest or where wildfire had burned about 25 years earlier. They then used computer simulations to estimate how the ground would have evolved after a fire. The results suggested that wildfire and extreme summer temperatures can warm and weaken the frozen ground surface, causing it to creep and form cracks.

More than 150 other slides in the region, identified via satellite observations, may also belong to this new category. According to Joseph Young, a permafrost geologist, such slides could occur wherever there is a relatively thin and warm permafrost layer and a rapid warming event to set things in motion. This implies that the hazard is not confined to a single valley but may be widespread across northern landscapes.

The implications are serious. A single slide can dam a river, causing floods upstream and disrupting fish migration. It can also sever transportation links, leaving communities isolated. As permafrost continues to thaw in cold regions worldwide, these huge slides are visual manifestations of a changing climate. Scientists say they need to better study what occurs beneath the surface, because the ground may move slowly or catastrophically.

long_sentences.en: Large landslides don’t normally mobilize so much still-frozen material, and when they do begin in thawing layers they usually move slowly, says Dmitry Nicolsky, a geophysicist studying permafrost at the University of Alaska Fairbanks who was not involved in the study.
These were the 2018 slide, which mobilized 18 million cubic meters of earth and dammed the Redstone River, and another event in 2017 that moved 4.5 million cubic meters of material.
That was surprising because they were in an area where the permafrost — ground that has been frozen for at least two consecutive years — shouldn’t have been thawing much.
